text: A waitress in Depression-era New Jersey buys the same ticket over and over, and the film files that under fantasy rather than habit. Cecilia has lost her job. Up on the screen, the archaeologist Tom Baxter goes about his adventure exactly as he did the previous afternoon, and will again tomorrow. Allen holds the whole thing to 82 minutes, so the comedy runs at the scale of the thing it is about: a short cheap show, seen twice. The Academy prize here went to the screenplay, which is the right address, since everything depends on how seriously a joke about moviegoing is prepared to take a person who has nothing else going. What is at stake is not the romance. It is the couple of hours a week that make the other hundred and sixty-six bearable.

An arranged marriage is being organized, and every person inside it wants something slightly different from the event. Nair runs five or six lines at once - a father under strain, a bride holding something back, an event planner gone quiet with infatuation - and lets them cut across each other rather than wait their turn. Hindi dialogue, French production money: the ordinary arrangement behind a certain kind of international film in 2001, and invisible in the result. Venice gave it the Golden Lion. What the 114 minutes actually turn on is the schedule - a date that cannot move, relatives arriving from wherever the family has scattered to, and a house in which nobody has anywhere left to have a private feeling in private.

A failure in one bedroom becomes, inside a year, the business of everyone with an opinion about the couple. Antonio loves Barbara, the marriage has gone unconsummated, and the household, the in-laws and the general estimate of a family's standing all arrive to take an interest. Bolognini plays this as domestic drama rather than scandal, which is the harder version, since it means watching two people stay fond of each other while the machinery around them treats the marriage as a case to be settled. The evasion is the style: the less plainly the thing is named, the louder the people around it get. Ninety-nine minutes, almost entirely talk. It carries a Golden Leopard, and the Italian list 100 film italiani da salvare keeps it on the books.

A fish seller in Naples takes Grande Fratello so seriously that he begins living as though the cameras were already running. Garrone gives that 117 minutes, which is long for a joke and about right for a condition, and the comedy belongs to the household around the man as much as to the man. Critics who write about Garrone tend to go after the sound; one study follows the sound space across his films, from fiction toward reality, and it is worth listening for here, since a person performing for an audience that is not in the room changes what the room does with noise. Cannes gave it the Grand Prix; the David di Donatello went to the direction. The premise would carry a farce, and the film keeps declining to make one.

The war is somewhere off the timetable, and at this village station the pressing business is an apprentice dispatcher's virginity. Menzel takes that ranking of concerns seriously rather than satirically, which is the whole method. Ninety-three minutes, mostly indoors, mostly the small talk of men whose work is to let other people's trains through occupied Czechoslovakia. The Academy's award for a foreign film went to it, and TIME's hundred has kept it in circulation since. The arithmetic underneath is quieter: the boy is oblivious, the resistance around him is not, and every hour he spends on his own frustration is an hour the world outside the depot spends on the war. The comedy never stops being funny while that sum runs.

An Academy Best Actress line and a Razzie for supporting actor sit on the same 122 minutes of film. Between them sits a boy whose family has been killed, a book the mob wants returned, and the neighbour who volunteered for none of it. Cassavetes starts a chase and then keeps stopping it - they have to eat, argue, find a bed, decide whether they can stand each other another hour. New York is shot at ground level, where a woman with a handbag and a child in tow is invisible or conspicuous depending on who is doing the looking. A Golden Lion and a place on TSPDT's thousand followed. Two hours is long for a pursuit, and the length is where her reluctance stops being a joke about babysitting and starts costing her something.

The whole machine is one man talking to another man, and one of them is lying. Welles brings the play down to 93 minutes, in English, on Italian production papers, and the compression leaves Iago's work looking like ordinary conversation held a little too close to the ear. Shakespeare on film usually swells; this version narrows. What survives the cutting is the tempo of suspicion - how few sentences it takes, how little evidence is required, how much of it the general supplies himself. It took the Palme d'Or, and it holds a place on TSPDT's thousand. The hardest position in the whole film is Desdemona's: asked to disprove a charge assembled out of nothing, by a husband who has already decided what the nothing means.

Two Russian soldiers are held in a mountain village as the price of one man's captured son. One has been in uniform long enough to calculate; the other is barely out of his boots. Bodrov keeps the film at the size of the house they are kept in - 99 minutes, a courtyard, chores, meals, and a father who set the arrangement up and takes no pleasure in running it. Almost nothing is explained about who is fighting whom, which leaves the captivity to be watched on its own terms, as a daily negotiation over whether a prisoner is a person or a receipt. The record is dense: an Academy line for international feature, the Crystal Globe, a European screenwriting award, a Nika for best picture. Everything rests on a proposition nobody says out loud, that one person can be traded for another, at par.

A man who has just given up fighting is handed a rifle by his government and told the objection has been noted. Hawks spends the long first stretch on the part most war pictures skip: the farm, the drinking, marksmanship as a country skill rather than a military one, and the conversion that turns all of it into a problem. Two hours and fourteen minutes is room enough for a moral argument to move at the speed people actually change their minds. The awards landed where the weight is, on the acting and on the black-and-white craft, art direction and cinematography. Released in 1941, it plainly had a second audience in mind besides Alvin York. What keeps it from being a recruiting pamphlet is that the objection is given its full hearing first, and is never made to look foolish.

A rich boy goes over the rail of an ocean liner and is pulled out of the Atlantic by men with no interest in whose son he is. The schooner does not turn around; there is a season's fishing to be done, and the captain offers wages instead of passage. That is the engine of it - not a rescue but a job, and the discovery that the currency the boy has used all his life is not accepted on the Grand Banks. Fleming films the boat as labour: weather, hours, a hierarchy a passenger has to find a place inside, 115 minutes in which nothing is corrected by an adult explaining it. The Academy record runs to Best Picture, Best Actor and editing, and the National Board of Review put it among the year's ten. The film is honest about how long it takes to stop being a nuisance.

Shining shoes for coins in postwar Rome adds up, eventually, to a horse. The horse is not a symbol of anything: it costs a sum, it is for sale, and two boys have decided to reach the sum. De Sica shot this in 1947, in a city still in the condition the war left, and his method is to take the children's economy entirely seriously: what things cost, who pays, which adult can be trusted with a transaction and which cannot. Ninety-one minutes, no cushioning. The Academy gave the screenplay a prize and the film an honorary one, and the National Board of Review put it among the year's ten best. The horse matters less than the arrangement behind it, two children who have decided to trust each other with money in a place where that is a serious decision.

Three people who owe a producer their careers sit down to describe what he did to them. The film is assembled from their accounts - a writer, a star, a director - so every scene arrives already interpreted by somebody with a grievance, and Minnelli lets the versions rub against one another. Hollywood filming Hollywood in 1952 could have been a settling of scores; this is more interested in the arithmetic of ambition, in how much of other people a man will spend to get a picture finished. The prizes for cinematography and art direction landed on a film whose subject is manufactured appearance, which is not an accident. The National Film Registry keeps it. Jonathan Shields is never explained away, and the refusal is what keeps three flashbacks from settling into a verdict.

A camera stays in one small village in northern Spain for a year, and the year is the entire structure. Álvarez works with 110 minutes and a place small enough to be filmed whole: the same fields under changing light, work that repeats because that is what work there does, talk that builds toward nothing. The discipline is in refusing to hurry a season. Documentary at this scale asks that duration be taken as information rather than delay, and the film keeps its end of the bargain by letting the seasons set the pace. A Tiger Award is on it, and Caimán's 100 mejores películas del cine español lists it. A year is the longest unit a small place can easily be held in, and nobody is obliged to come back and film the next one.

A collector's costume from a Japanese television series costs more than a father can raise honestly, and his daughter is running out of time to want it. Vermut builds 127 minutes on that gap. The premise sounds like sentiment and behaves like arithmetic - a price, a deadline, a city with an underside prepared to quote a figure for almost anything - which is why the genre line puts thriller beside drama. One academic reading takes the film as a study of capitalist magic and the sacred remedy set against it, a fair account of a story in which a wish carries an exact retail value. The Golden Shell, the IFFR audience award and a youth jury prize sit on its record. The costume is only the invoice. Underneath it sits a wish with a price attached, and a man who has decided to pay it.
